earlier_scan.note: Only ethnographic/subclassification refs on Glottolog (Singh 1994, Nambiar 1964, Varghese 2015); no phonological description located

sources.citation: Kalpana, S. & S. Gurugnanambiga. 2026. 'மலசர் பழங்குடிகளின் மலசமொழிப் பண்பாட்டியங்கியல் / Ethnolinguistic Cultural Dialectics of the Malasar Tribes.' International Journal of Tamil Language and Literary Studies (IJTLLS) 8(2), January 2026: 63-75. [Tamil, English abstract]. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18536961. (Avinashilingam Institute, Coimbatore; fieldwork Jan 2023-Dec 2024 in Malasar hamlets of Anaimalai, Pollachi, Kinathukadavu and Madukkarai taluks)
sources.note: No word-stress or tone statement. Two impressionistic prosodic remarks: (p.67) Malasar keeps some obsolete Old Tamil words and near-cognates 'with slightly different sound shape', and 'the pronunciation of the Malasa language also resembles Malayalam'; (p.70) because Malasar hamlets are traditionally dispersed rather than clustered, 'Malasa words contain sound-lengthened word structures and aḷapeṭai (vowel over-lengthening) suited to the open air' - i.e. a drawl / vowel prolongation, matching Nambiar 1964's 'peculiar accent and drawl' for the Mala Malasars, but nothing about the position of p…

sources.note: Catalog check only: OLAC lists just Glottolog, the Ethnologue entry and Varghese 2015; Glottolog has zero grammar/phonology/sketch references for either Malasar languoid (15 title hits, all ethnographic/overview/ISO change requests).

sources.note: Nothing on phonology: only 'Malasar is primarily an oral language which does not have a native script.. often transcribed in Tamil script', lexical similarity with Tamil, Malayalam, Muduga, Eravallan and Irula (citing Varghese 2015), frequent code-switching. WER 48% after Whisper fine-tuning.

sources.citation: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Scheme for Protection and Preservation of Endangered Languages (SPPEL). 'Malaimalasar' (endangered-language list sl. no. 62, Southern Zone, Kerala/Tamil Nadu) and 'Malasar Documentation' project page (grammar, Malasar-English-Tamil e-dictionary and ethnolinguistic profile announced as in progress; pilot survey done). Cf. Anthropological Survey of India Newsletter Jan-Mar 2015: AnSI officers supervising the CIIL study 'Protection and Preservation of Endangered Languages of two tribal communities, namely Malai Malasar & Muduvan'.
sources.note: No linguistic content online: page says Malasar is 'an unclassified southern language', speakers 'converse with each other in a patois debased form of Tamil', and that a grammar and trilingual dictionary are planned. No grammatical-sketch or grammatical-features page exists for Malasar/Malaimalasar (checked all SPPEL resource lists).

sources.citation: Varghese, Bijumon (comp.). 2015. The Tribes of Palakkad, Kerala: A Sociolinguistic Profile. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2015-028. Dallas: SIL International. 173 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic survey (lexical similarity, RTT, SRT, language-use questionnaires). Sec. 1.3 (p.2) and 2.5 'Mala Malasar' (pp.10-11) only say the group 'speak a dialect of Tamil, officially described as "Malasir"' (citing Menon 1996:196). Appendix B gives one 210-item IPA wordlist from Mala Malasar, Ancham Colony (Chittoor taluk) with no stress marks; p.47 states the wordlists are field transcriptions that 'have not undergone thorough phonological and grammatical analysis'. Zero hits for stress/accent/suprasegmental/prosody in the full text.

sources.citation: Chandi, Manish. 2008. Tribes of the Anamalais: livelihood and resource-use patterns of communities in the rainforests of the Indira Gandhi Wildlife Sanctuary and Valparai plateau. NCF Technical Report No. 16. Mysore: Nature Conservation Foundation. 90 pp.
sources.note: No phonology content; ethnographic/livelihood report. Only says the three tribes 'are distinguished by dialects and customs' and that Malai Malasars 'differ in language and geographical location' from Malasars (pers. comm.).

sources.citation: Menon, T. Madhava (chief ed.). 1996. The Encyclopaedia of Dravidian Tribes, Vol. II. Thiruvananthapuram: International School of Dravidian Linguistics. Entry 'MAHA MALASAR' by Jakka Parthasarathy, pp.195-197 (and 'MALASAR', pp.238-241).
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnographic entry; the only language statement (p.196): 'They speak a dialect of Tamil, officially described as "Malasir". A few of them also know Malayalam.' The Malasar entry (p.240) says only 'They speak Tamil; a few know Malayalam and Kannada.'

sources.citation: Nambiar, P. K. 1964. Census of India 1961, Volume IX Madras, Part V-B (I): Ethnographic Notes on Scheduled Tribes (Muduvars, Kadars, Kanis or Kanikkars, Mala Malasars, Paniyans, Palliyans, Mullu Kurumbars). Madras: Superintendent of Census Operations. 328 pp. [Ch. 4 'Mala Malasars', pp. 139-150]
sources.note: Only an impressionistic remark, verbatim: 'The mother tongue of Mala Malasars is Tamil which they speak with a peculiar accent and drawl. Their vocabulary contains a few Malayalam words also. A newcomer would find it difficult to follow their conversation, because of the accent and drawl.' No phoneme inventory, no vocabulary list, nothing on word-stress position or tone. ('accent' here = manner of pronunciation, not word accent.)

sources.citation: Aiyappan, A. 1948. Report on the Socio-Economic Conditions of the Aboriginal Tribes of the Province of Madras. Madras: Government Press. (section 'MALASARS', Coimbatore district hill tribes; archive.org item;ernet.dli.2015.215992)
sources.note: No phonology content; the whole language statement is one clause: 'They speak a patois of Tamil'. The rest of the section is census figures (1941: 8,441 Coimbatore + 2,161 Malabar), sub-divisions (Nattu / Kongu Malayans; Malai Malasars of Mount Stuart), settlement (padi/pati), economy, marriage and religion. No vocabulary.

sources.note: No Malasar section. States only that Malasar and Malamalasar (with Kollimalai/Pachaimalai/Kalvarayan Malayali, Urali Sholaga) 'speak their (Tamil) dialects' ('தங்கள் (தமிழின்) கிளை மொழிகளைப் பேசுகிறார்கள்'), and quotes Ananthakrishna Iyer 1909 that Anaimalai Kadars speak 'a kind of Tamil called Malasar'. The book's phonological sketches cover Toda, Kota, Irula, Paniya, Kurumba varieties, Kadar, Kasaba - not Malasar.
